{"markdown": "Sound model testing includes a critical assessment of data quality, relevance, and inputs, and this section sets out the evidence available on that point for the credit_default package at version 1.0 [[reg:SR26-2:IV.1]].

The training split holds 3500 [[art:2510d49d:profile.train.n]] rows and the test split holds 1500 [[art:2193cf5f:profile.test.n]] rows.

### Missingness

The largest missing fraction of any column in the training split is 0 [[art:050a3099:profile.train.missing.max]].
The largest missing fraction of any column in the test split is also 0 [[art:f813848d:profile.test.missing.max]].
Because the two split maxima coincide, there is no gap between them to speak of, and it therefore sits inside the tolerated between-split missingness gap of 0.1 [[art:9cce25ea:threshold.D1.missing_gap]].
No column in either split is carrying imputed or absent values that could differ in prevalence from one split to the other.

### Population and characteristic stability

The largest train-to-test population stability index, taken across the features and the score together, is 0.01095 [[art:381b2570:psi.max]], which is read against the declared stability bound of 0.25 [[art:278b9016:threshold.S1.psi]] and lies far inside it.
That bound is the same value the package itself declares, 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]], so the bound applied in review and the bound declared by the developer agree.
The feature-by-feature population stability indices between the training and test splits are as follows.

- age: 0.008124 [[art:f9255a0a:psi.age]]
- bill_mean_6m: 0.007124 [[art:028e4281:psi.bill_mean_6m]]
- bill_trend_6m: 0.00958 [[art:c247a6f2:psi.bill_trend_6m]]
- delinq_count_6m: 0.002069 [[art:61491d02:psi.delinq_count_6m]]
- delinq_last: 0.00285 [[art:03bd52e7:psi.delinq_last]]
- delinq_max_6m: 0.005498 [[art:7a82e7f3:psi.delinq_max_6m]]
- limit_bal: 0.01095 [[art:601cdba2:psi.limit_bal]]
- pay_ratio_last: 0.004966 [[art:3af2ca29:psi.pay_ratio_last]]
- pay_ratio_mean_6m: 0.0055 [[art:2c5baeb2:psi.pay_ratio_mean_6m]]
- utilisation: 0.004244 [[art:451e0780:psi.utilisation]]

The credit-limit feature is the one that attains the overall maximum, at 0.01095 [[art:601cdba2:psi.limit_bal]], and every other feature shift is smaller still.
The score distribution itself moves by 0.007023 [[art:a2885abf:psi.y_score]] between the two splits, so the shift the model sees in its own output is of the same small order as the shifts in its inputs.

Characteristic stability, measured as each feature's contribution to the shift in the linear predictor, is reported next.

- age: 0.0009476 [[art:a78e58f6:csi.age]]
- bill_mean_6m: 0.002369 [[art:48df6cc9:csi.bill_mean_6m]]
- bill_trend_6m: 0.00633 [[art:59948e6d:csi.bill_trend_6m]]
- delinq_count_6m: 0.002449 [[art:69346f52:csi.delinq_count_6m]]
- delinq_last: 0.02363 [[art:5babe364:csi.delinq_last]]
- delinq_max_6m: 0.0008965 [[art:7244960d:csi.delinq_max_6m]]
- limit_bal: 0.001211 [[art:5b77b34b:csi.limit_bal]]
- pay_ratio_last: 0.001924 [[art:aff2b4bf:csi.pay_ratio_last]]
- pay_ratio_mean_6m: 0.001768 [[art:f567818e:csi.pay_ratio_mean_6m]]
- utilisation: 0.004042 [[art:10f0f9e7:csi.utilisation]]

The largest of these contributions is 0.02363 [[art:e56cb179:csi.max]], carried by the most recent delinquency indicator at 0.02363 [[art:5babe364:csi.delinq_last]], and it too remains well inside the declared stability bound of 0.25 [[art:278b9016:threshold.S1.psi]].
The distribution of contributions is not concentrated in a single input, and the largest single contribution is roughly twice the next largest rather than an order of magnitude above it.

### Leakage and contamination screens

The timing screen counts 0 [[art:742bcd24:leakage.timing.n_flagged]] features whose declared observation window falls during the performance period or after the outcome is known, so the declared timings raise nothing on their own.
The timing evidence rests on the developer's declarations rather than on independent inspection of the source systems, and it is only as good as those declarations.
The strongest single feature reaches an area under the curve of 0.6831 [[art:fd829fc4:leakage.target_corr.max_single_feature_auc]] on its own, against the bound of 0.9 [[art:c29e7a34:threshold.L1.single_feature_auc]] above which a lone predictor would be treated as target-adjacent, so no individual input carries near-outcome information.
The share of test rows whose feature values also appear in the training split is 0 [[art:4c9fcd09:leakage.overlap]].

The contamination screen has two arms, each read against its own bound.
On the identifier arm, the share of test rows whose client identifier also identifies a training row is 0 [[art:63d37fc5:leakage.overlap.ids]], against the declared contamination bound of 0.005 [[art:9f336eaf:threshold.L2.overlap]].
On the feature-vector arm, the share of test rows whose feature values also appear in the training split is 0 [[art:0fec8048:leakage.overlap.features]], and the bound that arm actually applied is 0.005 [[art:1ee888c5:threshold.L2.overlap.features_effective]].
That effective bound is the larger of the declared contamination bound and twice the share of training rows whose feature values are not unique within the training split, which is 0 [[art:4474c227:leakage.duplicates.train]]; because no training rows duplicate one another on features, the widening term contributes nothing and the effective bound equals the declared one.
The reason for widening the feature-vector arm in that way is that two distinct subjects can coincide on a discrete feature vector by chance, and such a coincidence is not evidence that the same subject appears on both sides of the split.
Here the question does not arise, since both arms return no overlap at all.
The name screen matches 0 [[art:407e62be:leakage.name_screen.n_matched]] feature names against the target-adjacent lexicon, so no input is flagged by its name as a restatement of the outcome.

### Assessment

On the evidence assembled here, the two splits are alike in missingness, the population and characteristic shifts between them are one to two orders of magnitude inside the declared bound, and none of the leakage or contamination screens registers an exceedance against the bound it was read against.
The screens are structural rather than semantic: they test identifier and feature-vector coincidence, the discriminatory power of single inputs, and declared timings, and they would not detect an input that encodes the outcome through a legitimate-looking upstream transformation.
The stability evidence covers the training and test splits as reported above, and the strength of the conclusion is limited by the size of the test split relative to the training split."}

You are drafting one section of a model-validation report on the model package credit_default version
1.0. The report follows the structure of the Federal Reserve's model risk management
guidance and never claims compliance with it.

Section: ## 3. Data integrity and drift

What this section must do:
Assess the data: missingness in each split and the gap between them against its threshold,
population and characteristic stability between the training split and the others against the
declared bound, and each leakage screen -- declared timings, the strongest single feature against
the leakage threshold, the share of test rows that also appear in train, and the name screen.
The contamination screen has two arms and each is read against its own bound. Compare
leakage.overlap.ids with threshold.L2.overlap, and compare leakage.overlap.features with
threshold.L2.overlap.features_effective, which is the bound that rule actually applied: it is the
larger of threshold.L2.overlap and twice leakage.duplicates.train, because two different subjects
writing the same discrete row is coincidence rather than contamination. Cite whichever bound you
compare a number against, and do not compare a feature-vector overlap with the declared
threshold.

Rules, all of them checked after you answer:
- Every number you write is followed immediately by its [[art:...]] citation, copied exactly from
  the JSON below. A number with no citation is counted against this report.
- Write no number that is not in the JSON below. If you want to say something the artifacts do not
  support, say it in words without a number.
- The artifacts below are **this section's selection, not the store**. Never write that a quantity
  is absent, uncomputed, not recomputed, not available or "not carried": another section may hold
  it, and a report that says one section's selection is the whole run contradicts itself. Say what
  the numbers you have show, and where you need one you were not given, write the sentence without
  it.
- Do not write an artifact's logical name in the prose. The citation after the number carries it,
  and a sentence that also spells it out reads "by up to threshold.O1.slice_auc_gap at 0.08" where
  it should read "by up to 0.08 [[art:...:threshold.O1.slice_auc_gap]]". Say in words what the
  number is, and let the citation say where it came from.
- One sentence per line. The claim extractor works line by line, so a sentence split over two
  lines is two claims and a paragraph on one line is one.
- For a table artifact, do not retype the cells. Write the directive [[table:<logical_name>]] on a
  line of its own; the renderer expands it, with its caption and its citation, from the store.
- Open the section with a sentence that anchors it to the guidance, carrying one [[reg:...]]
  citation copied from the guidance spans below. Prefer a span of the current guidance, SR26-2;
  cite the superseded SR11-7 only where it says something the revision does not.
- Write markdown. Do not write a level-2 heading: the renderer writes it.
- Do not use the words "compliant" or "certified".
- Call something a finding only if it is in the candidate list at the end of this prompt. The
  findings section reports exactly that list, and a section that calls anything else a finding
  contradicts it.

  "text": "For the purposes of this document, the term model refers to a quantitative method,\nsystem, or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories,\ntechniques, and assumptions to process input data into quantitative estimates. The definition of model also covers\nquantitative approaches whose inputs are partially or wholly qualitative or based on\nexpert judgment, provided that the output is quantitative in nature. For example, precision and accuracy are relevant for models that forecast future\nvalues, while discriminatory power applies to models that rank order risks. In all\nsituations, it is important to understand a model's capabilities and limitations given its\nsimplifications and assumptions.\nThe use of models invariably presents model risk, which is the potential for adverse\nconsequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports.\nModel risk can lead to financial loss, poor business and strategic decision making, or\ndamage to a bank's reputation. Model risk occurs primarily for two reasons:\n\u2022 The model may have fundamental errors and may produce inaccurate outputs\nwhen viewed against the design objective and intended business uses. The\nmathematical calculation and quantification exercise underlying any model\ngenerally involves application of theory, choice of sample design and numerical\nroutines, selection of inputs and estimation, and implementation in information\nsystems. Errors can occur at any point from design through implementation. In\naddition, shortcuts, simplifications, or approximations used to manage\ncomplicated problems could compromise the integrity and reliability of outputs [Page Break]\nfrom those calculations. Finally, the quality of model outputs depends on the\nquality of input data and assumptions, and errors in inputs or incorrect\nassumptions will lead to inaccurate outputs.\n\u2022 The model may be used incorrectly or inappropriately. Even a fundamentally\nsound model producing accurate outputs consistent with the design objective of\nthe model may exhibit high model risk if it is misapplied or misused. Models by\ntheir nature are simplifications of reality, and real-world events may prove those\nsimplifications inappropriate. This is even more of a concern if a model is used\noutside the environment for which it was designed. Banks may do this\nintentionally as they apply existing models to new products or markets, or\ninadvertently as market conditions or customer behavior changes. Decision\nmakers need to understand the limitations of a model to avoid using it in ways\nthat are not consistent with the original intent. Limitations come in part from\nweaknesses in the model due to its various shortcomings, approximations, and\nuncertainties. Limitations are also a consequence of assumptions underlying a\nmodel that may restrict the scope to a limited set of specific circumstances and\nsituations.\nModel risk should be managed like other types of risk. Banks should identify the sources\nof risk and assess the magnitude. Model risk increases with greater model complexity,\nhigher uncertainty about inputs and assumptions, broader use, and larger potential impact.\nBanks should consider risk from individual models and in the aggregate. Aggregate\nmodel risk is affected by interaction and dependencies among models; reliance on\ncommon assumptions, data, or methodologies; and any other factors that could adversely\naffect several models and their outputs at the same time. With an understanding of the\nsource and magnitude of model risk in place, the next step is to manage it properly.\nA guiding principle for managing model risk is \"effective challenge\" of models, that is,\ncritical analysis by objective, informed parties who can identify model limitations and\nassumptions and produce appropriate changes. Effective challenge depends on a\ncombination of incentives, competence, and influence. Incentives to provide effective\nchallenge to models are stronger when there is greater separation of that challenge from\nthe model development process and when challenge is supported by well-designed\ncompensation practices and corporate culture. Competence is a key to effectiveness since\ntechnical knowledge and modeling skills are necessary to conduct appropriate analysis\nand critique. Finally, challenge may fail to be effective without the influence to ensure\nthat actions are taken to address model issues.   "text": "The third core element of the validation process is outcomes analysis, a comparison of\nmodel outputs to corresponding actual outcomes. The precise nature of the comparison\ndepends on the objectives of a model, and might include an assessment of the accuracy of\nestimates or forecasts, an evaluation of rank-ordering ability, or other appropriate tests. In\nall cases, such comparisons help to evaluate model performance, by establishing expected\nranges for those actual outcomes in relation to the intended objectives and assessing the\nreasons for observed variation between the two. If outcomes analysis produces evidence\nof poor performance, the bank should take action to address those issues. Outcomes\nanalysis typically relies on statistical tests or other quantitative measures. It can also [Page Break]\ninclude expert judgment to check the intuition behind the outcomes and confirm that the\nresults make sense. When a model itself relies on expert judgment, quantitative outcomes\nanalysis helps to evaluate the quality of that judgment. Outcomes analysis should be\nconducted on an ongoing basis to test whether the model continues to perform in line\nwith design objectives and business uses.\nA variety of quantitative and qualitative testing and analytical techniques can be used in\noutcomes analysis. The choice of technique should be based on the model's\nmethodology, its complexity, data availability, and the magnitude of potential model risk\nto the bank. Outcomes analysis should involve a range of tests because any individual test\nwill have weaknesses. For example, some tests are better at checking a model's ability to\nrank-order or segment observations on a relative basis, whereas others are better at\nchecking absolute forecast accuracy. Tests should be designed for each situation, as not\nall will be effective or feasible in every circumstance, and attention should be paid to\nchoosing the appropriate type of outcomes analysis for a particular model.\nModels are regularly adjusted to take into account new data or techniques, or because of\ndeterioration in performance. Parallel outcomes analysis, under which both the original\nand adjusted models' forecasts are tested against realized outcomes, provides an\nimportant test of such model adjustments. If the adjusted model does not outperform the\noriginal model, developers, users, and reviewers should realize that additional changes\u2014\nor even a wholesale redesign\u2014are likely necessary before the adjusted model replaces\nthe original one.\nBack-testing is one form of outcomes analysis; specifically, it involves the comparison of\nactual outcomes with model forecasts during a sample time period not used in model\ndevelopment and at an observation frequency that matches the forecast horizon or\nperformance window of the model. The comparison is generally done using expected\nranges or statistical confidence intervals around the model forecasts. When outcomes fall\noutside those intervals, the bank should analyze the discrepancies and investigate the\ncauses that are significant in terms of magnitude or frequency. The objective of the\nanalysis is to determine whether differences stem from the omission of material factors\nfrom the model, whether they arise from errors with regard to other aspects of model\nspecification such as interaction terms or assumptions of linearity, or whether they are\npurely random and thus consistent with acceptable model performance. Analysis of in-\nsample fit and of model performance in holdout samples (data set aside and not used to\nestimate the original model) are important parts of model development but are not\nsubstitutes for back-testing.\nA well-known example of back-testing is the evaluation of value-at-risk (VaR), in which\nactual profit and loss is compared with a model forecast loss distribution. Significant\ndeviation in expected versus actual performance and unexplained volatility in the profits\nand losses of trading activities may indicate that hedging and pricing relationships are not\nadequately measured by a given approach. Along with measuring the frequency of losses\nin excess of a single VaR percentile estimator, banks should use other tests, such as [Page Break]\nassessing any clustering of exceptions and checking the distribution of losses against\nother estimated percentiles.\nAnalysis of the results of even high-quality and well-designed back-testing can pose\nchallenges, since it is not a straightforward, mechanical process that always produces\nunambiguous results. The purpose is to test the model, not individual forecast values.\nBack-testing may entail analysis of a large number of forecasts over different conditions\nat a point in time or over multiple time periods. Statistical testing is essential in such\ncases, yet such testing can pose challenges in both the choice of appropriate tests and the\ninterpretation of results; banks should support and document both the choice of tests and\nthe interpretation of results.\nModels with long forecast horizons should be back-tested, but given the amount of time it\nwould take to accumulate the necessary data, that testing should be supplemented by\nevaluation over shorter periods. Banks should employ outcomes analysis consisting of\n\"early warning\" metrics designed to measure performance beginning very shortly after\nmodel introduction and trend analysis of performance over time. These outcomes analysis\ntools are not substitutes for back-testing, which should still be performed over the longer\ntime period, but rather very important complements.\nOutcomes analysis and the other elements of the validation process may reveal significant\nerrors or inaccuracies in model development or outcomes that consistently fall outside the\nbank's predetermined thresholds of acceptability. In such cases, model adjustment,\nrecalibration, or redevelopment is warranted. Adjustments and recalibration should be\ngoverned by the principle of conservatism and should undergo independent review.\nMaterial changes in model structure or technique, and all model redevelopment, should\nbe subject to validation activities of appropriate range and rigor before implementation.\nAt times banks may have a limited ability to use key model validation tools like back-\ntesting or sensitivity analysis for various reasons, such as lack of data or of price\nobservability. {"markdown": "Sound development practice includes a critical assessment of data quality, relevance, and inputs, and this section reviews that evidence for the credit default package [[reg:SR26-2:IV.1]].

The training split holds 3500 [[art:2510d49d:profile.train.n]] rows and the test split holds 1500 [[art:2193cf5f:profile.test.n]] rows.
The largest missing fraction in any training column is 0 [[art:050a3099:profile.train.missing.max]], and the largest in any test column is likewise 0 [[art:f813848d:profile.test.missing.max]].
Because the two splits are complete to the same degree, the gap in missingness between them is nil and sits inside the permitted gap of 0.1 [[art:9cce25ea:threshold.D1.missing_gap]].

Population stability from training to test is bounded at 0.25 [[art:278b9016:threshold.S1.psi]], the same figure the package declares at 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]].
The largest train-to-test population stability index, score included, is 0.01095 [[art:381b2570:psi.max]], roughly a twentieth of that bound.
The per-feature population stability indices between training and test are as follows.

- limit_bal: 0.01095 [[art:601cdba2:psi.limit_bal]]
- bill_trend_6m: 0.00958 [[art:c247a6f2:psi.bill_trend_6m]]
- age: 0.008124 [[art:f9255a0a:psi.age]]
- bill_mean_6m: 0.007124 [[art:028e4281:psi.bill_mean_6m]]
- the model score: 0.007023 [[art:a2885abf:psi.y_score]]
- pay_ratio_mean_6m: 0.0055 [[art:2c5baeb2:psi.pay_ratio_mean_6m]]
- delinq_max_6m: 0.005498 [[art:7a82e7f3:psi.delinq_max_6m]]
- pay_ratio_last: 0.004966 [[art:3af2ca29:psi.pay_ratio_last]]
- utilisation: 0.004244 [[art:451e0780:psi.utilisation]]
- delinq_last: 0.00285 [[art:03bd52e7:psi.delinq_last]]
- delinq_count_6m: 0.002069 [[art:61491d02:psi.delinq_count_6m]]

No single feature moves the population enough to approach the declared bound, and the score itself shifts less than several of its inputs, which is consistent with a stable scored population rather than with offsetting drift.

Characteristic stability, read as each feature's contribution to the shift in the linear predictor, is largest for delinq_last at 0.02363 [[art:5babe364:csi.delinq_last]], which is also the largest such contribution overall at 0.02363 [[art:e56cb179:csi.max]].
Measured against the declared stability bound of 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]], that largest contribution is smaller by an order of magnitude, and every other contribution is smaller still.
The per-feature characteristic stability contributions are as follows.

- delinq_last: 0.02363 [[art:5babe364:csi.delinq_last]]
- bill_trend_6m: 0.00633 [[art:59948e6d:csi.bill_trend_6m]]
- utilisation: 0.004042 [[art:10f0f9e7:csi.utilisation]]
- delinq_count_6m: 0.002449 [[art:69346f52:csi.delinq_count_6m]]
- bill_mean_6m: 0.002369 [[art:48df6cc9:csi.bill_mean_6m]]
- pay_ratio_last: 0.001924 [[art:aff2b4bf:csi.pay_ratio_last]]
- pay_ratio_mean_6m: 0.001768 [[art:f567818e:csi.pay_ratio_mean_6m]]
- limit_bal: 0.001211 [[art:5b77b34b:csi.limit_bal]]
- age: 0.0009476 [[art:a78e58f6:csi.age]]
- delinq_max_6m: 0.0008965 [[art:7244960d:csi.delinq_max_6m]]

It is worth noting that delinq_last contributes the largest share of the predictor shift while ranking only mid-table on population movement, so the delinquency block is where a reviewer should look first if drift is monitored after deployment.

Four leakage screens were run over the training and test splits.
The declared-timing screen flags 0 [[art:742bcd24:leakage.timing.n_flagged]] features as observed during the performance period or after the outcome, so the input set is declared to be knowable at scoring time.
The strongest single feature reaches an area under the curve of 0.6831 [[art:fd829fc4:leakage.target_corr.max_single_feature_auc]] on its own, comfortably below the 0.9 [[art:c29e7a34:threshold.L1.single_feature_auc]] that any one feature is permitted to reach, so no individual input behaves like a restatement of the target.
The name screen matches 0 [[art:407e62be:leakage.name_screen.n_matched]] feature names against the target-adjacent lexicon.

The contamination screen has two arms, and each is read against its own bound.
On the identifier arm, the share of test rows whose client identifier also identifies a training row is 0 [[art:63d37fc5:leakage.overlap.ids]], against the declared bound of 0.005 [[art:9f336eaf:threshold.L2.overlap]].
On the feature-vector arm, the share of test rows whose feature values also appear in training is 0 [[art:0fec8048:leakage.overlap.features]], read against the bound the rule actually applied, 0.005 [[art:1ee888c5:threshold.L2.overlap.features_effective]].
That applied bound is the larger of the declared overlap fraction and twice the share of training rows whose feature values are not unique within training, which is 0 [[art:4474c227:leakage.duplicates.train]], on the reasoning that two different subjects writing the same discrete row is coincidence rather than contamination.
Because duplication within training is nil, the applied bound coincides with the declared one here, and the feature-vector arm would have been read the same way under either.

Taken together, the splits are complete, the population and the individual characteristics move little between training and test relative to the declared bound, and none of the four leakage screens or either contamination arm exceeds the bound it was read against."}

  "heading": "Overview of Model Risk Management",
  "text": "For the purposes of this document, the term model refers to a quantitative method,\nsystem, or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories,\ntechniques, and assumptions to process input data into quantitative estimates. [Footnote 3\n- While outside the scope of this guidance, more qualitative approaches used by banking organizations\u2014\ni.e., those not defined as models according to this guidance\u2014should also be subject to a rigorous control\nprocess. For example, precision and accuracy are relevant for models that forecast future\nvalues, while discriminatory power applies to models that rank order risks. In all\nsituations, it is important to understand a model's capabilities and limitations given its\nsimplifications and assumptions.\nThe use of models invariably presents model risk, which is the potential for adverse\nconsequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports.\nModel risk can lead to financial loss, poor business and strategic decision making, or\ndamage to a bank's reputation. Model risk occurs primarily for two reasons:\n\u2022 The model may have fundamental errors and may produce inaccurate outputs\nwhen viewed against the design objective and intended business uses. The\nmathematical calculation and quantification exercise underlying any model\ngenerally involves application of theory, choice of sample design and numerical\nroutines, selection of inputs and estimation, and implementation in information\nsystems. Errors can occur at any point from design through implementation. In\naddition, shortcuts, simplifications, or approximations used to manage\ncomplicated problems could compromise the integrity and reliability of outputs [Page Break]\nfrom those calculations. Finally, the quality of model outputs depends on the\nquality of input data and assumptions, and errors in inputs or incorrect\nassumptions will lead to inaccurate outputs.\n\u2022 The model may be used incorrectly or inappropriately. {"markdown": "Sound development practice includes a critical assessment of data quality, relevance, and inputs, and this section reviews the evidence supporting that assessment for the candidate package [[reg:SR26-2:IV.1]].

### Splits and missingness

The training split holds 3500 [[art:2510d49d:profile.train.n]] rows and the test split holds 1500 [[art:2193cf5f:profile.test.n]] rows.
The largest missing fraction in any training column is 0 [[art:050a3099:profile.train.missing.max]], and the largest missing fraction in any test column is 0 [[art:2193cf5f:profile.test.n]].
Both splits are therefore complete on every column screened, so the difference in missingness between them is nil and sits well inside the bound of 0.1 [[art:9cce25ea:threshold.D1.missing_gap]] that governs the gap.

### Population and characteristic stability

The largest train-to-test population stability index, the score included, is 0.01095 [[art:381b2570:psi.max]], against a declared bound of 0.25 [[art:278b9016:threshold.S1.psi]], which is the same value the package itself declares at 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]].
The margin is better than an order of magnitude, so the two splits are drawn from populations that are close to indistinguishable on the screened marginals.

The per-feature population stability indices are as follows.

- age: 0.008124 [[art:f9255a0a:psi.age]]
- limit_bal: 0.01095 [[art:601cdba2:psi.limit_bal]]
- utilisation: 0.004244 [[art:451e0780:psi.utilisation]]
- pay_ratio_last: 0.004966 [[art:3af2ca29:psi.pay_ratio_last]]
- pay_ratio_mean_6m: 0.0055 [[art:2c5baeb2:psi.pay_ratio_mean_6m]]
- bill_mean_6m: 0.007124 [[art:028e4281:psi.bill_mean_6m]]
- bill_trend_6m: 0.00958 [[art:c247a6f2:psi.bill_trend_6m]]
- delinq_last: 0.00285 [[art:03bd52e7:psi.delinq_last]]
- delinq_max_6m: 0.005498 [[art:7a82e7f3:psi.delinq_max_6m]]
- delinq_count_6m: 0.002069 [[art:61491d02:psi.delinq_count_6m]]
- the model score: 0.007023 [[art:a2885abf:psi.y_score]]

The largest of these is the balance-limit shift at 0.01095 [[art:601cdba2:psi.limit_bal]], which is also the run-wide maximum, so no single input drives the aggregate figure.

Characteristic stability, which weights each feature's shift by its contribution to the linear predictor, reaches at most 0.02363 [[art:e56cb179:csi.max]].
That maximum is contributed by the most recent delinquency indicator at 0.02363 [[art:5babe364:csi.delinq_last]], a feature whose own marginal shift is only 0.00285 [[art:03bd52e7:psi.delinq_last]], so the contribution reflects the weight the model places on it rather than a large movement in the input itself.

The remaining per-feature characteristic stability contributions are as follows.

- age: 0.0009476 [[art:a78e58f6:csi.age]]
- limit_bal: 0.001211 [[art:5b77b34b:csi.limit_bal]]
- utilisation: 0.004042 [[art:10f0f9e7:csi.utilisation]]
- pay_ratio_last: 0.001924 [[art:aff2b4bf:csi.pay_ratio_last]]
- pay_ratio_mean_6m: 0.001768 [[art:f567818e:csi.pay_ratio_mean_6m]]
- bill_mean_6m: 0.002369 [[art:48df6cc9:csi.bill_mean_6m]]
- bill_trend_6m: 0.00633 [[art:59948e6d:csi.bill_trend_6m]]
- delinq_max_6m: 0.0008965 [[art:7244960d:csi.delinq_max_6m]]
- delinq_count_6m: 0.002449 [[art:69346f52:csi.delinq_count_6m]]

Every contribution outside the delinquency indicator sits an order of magnitude or more below the aggregate stability bound of 0.25 [[art:278b9016:threshold.S1.psi]].

### Leakage screens

Four screens were run against the feature set, and each is reported below with the bound it was read against.

The timing screen counts features declared as observed during the performance period or after the outcome, and it flags 0 [[art:742bcd24:leakage.timing.n_flagged]] of them, so no declared timing places an input after the event it is meant to predict.
This screen rests on the declared timings rather than on an independent reconstruction of when each field was written, and it is only as strong as those declarations.

The strongest single feature reaches an area under the curve of 0.6831 [[art:fd829fc4:leakage.target_corr.max_single_feature_auc]] on its own, against a bound of 0.9 [[art:c29e7a34:threshold.L1.single_feature_auc]].
No individual input therefore comes close to reproducing the target by itself, which is the pattern a directly leaked field would show.

The contamination screen has two arms, each read against its own bound.
The share of test rows whose identifiers also identify a row of train is 0 [[art:63d37fc5:leakage.overlap.ids]], against the declared bound of 0.005 [[art:9f336eaf:threshold.L2.overlap]], so no subject appears on both sides of the split.
The share of test rows whose feature values also appear in train is 0 [[art:0fec8048:leakage.overlap.features]], read against the bound the feature arm actually applied, 0.005 [[art:1ee888c5:threshold.L2.overlap.features_effective]].
That effective bound is the larger of the declared bound and twice the share of train rows whose feature values are not unique within train, which is 0 [[art:4474c227:leakage.duplicates.train]]; because train contains no repeated feature vectors, the relaxation contributes nothing and the effective bound coincides with the declared one.
The relaxation exists because two distinct subjects may write identical values on a set of discrete fields by coincidence, and such collisions should not be charged to the split as contamination.
The overall share of test rows whose feature values also appear in train is likewise 0 [[art:4c9fcd09:leakage.overlap]], consistent with both arms.

The name screen matches feature names against a lexicon of target-adjacent terms and returns 0 [[art:407e62be:leakage.name_screen.n_matched]] matches.
A name screen detects only leakage that is announced in the naming, so it corroborates the other screens rather than standing on its own.

### Assessment

On the evidence assembled here, the two splits are complete, closely matched in distribution both marginally and after weighting by model influence, and free of the identifier and feature-vector overlap that would let training information reach the test split.
The residual risk in this area is concentrated in the timing declarations and the name lexicon, both of which depend on inputs supplied by the developer rather than on properties recovered from the data, and reviewers relying on this section should weigh those two screens accordingly."}

  "heading": "Overview of Model Risk Management",
  "text": "For the purposes of this document, the term model refers to a quantitative method,\nsystem, or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories,\ntechniques, and assumptions to process input data into quantitative estimates. A model\nconsists of three components: an information input component, which delivers\nassumptions and data to the model; a processing component, which transforms inputs into\nestimates; and a reporting component, which translates the estimates into useful business\ninformation. Models meeting this definition might be used for analyzing business\nstrategies, informing business decisions, identifying and measuring risks, valuing\nexposures, instruments or positions, conducting stress testing, assessing adequacy of\ncapital, managing client assets, measuring compliance with internal limits, maintaining\nthe formal control apparatus of the bank, or meeting financial or regulatory reporting\nrequirements and issuing public disclosures. The definition of model also covers\nquantitative approaches whose inputs are partially or wholly qualitative or based on\nexpert judgment, provided that the output is quantitative in nature. [Footnote 3\n- While outside the scope of this guidance, more qualitative approaches used by banking organizations\u2014\ni.e., those not defined as models according to this guidance\u2014should also be subject to a rigorous control\nprocess. End of Footnote 3.]\nModels are simplified representations of real-world relationships among observed\ncharacteristics, values, and events. Simplification is inevitable, due to the inherent\ncomplexity of those relationships, but also intentional, to focus attention on particular\naspects considered to be most important for a given model application. Model quality can\nbe measured in many ways: precision, accuracy, discriminatory power, robustness,\nstability, and reliability, to name a few. Models are never perfect, and the appropriate\nmetrics of quality, and the effort that should be put into improving quality, depend on the\nsituation. For example, precision and accuracy are relevant for models that forecast future\nvalues, while discriminatory power applies to models that rank order risks. In all\nsituations, it is important to understand a model's capabilities and limitations given its\nsimplifications and assumptions.\nThe use of models invariably presents model risk, which is the potential for adverse\nconsequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports.\nModel risk can lead to financial loss, poor business and strategic decision making, or\ndamage to a bank's reputation. Model risk occurs primarily for two reasons:\n\u2022 The model may have fundamental errors and may produce inaccurate outputs\nwhen viewed against the design objective and intended business uses. The\nmathematical calculation and quantification exercise underlying any model\ngenerally involves application of theory, choice of sample design and numerical\nroutines, selection of inputs and estimation, and implementation in information\nsystems. Errors can occur at any point from design through implementation. In\naddition, shortcuts, simplifications, or approximations used to manage\ncomplicated problems could compromise the integrity and reliability of outputs [Page Break]\nfrom those calculations. Finally, the quality of model outputs depends on the\nquality of input data and assumptions, and errors in inputs or incorrect\nassumptions will lead to inaccurate outputs.\n\u2022 The model may be used incorrectly or inappropriately. Even a fundamentally\nsound model producing accurate outputs consistent with the design objective of\nthe model may exhibit high model risk if it is misapplied or misused. Models by\ntheir nature are simplifications of reality, and real-world events may prove those\nsimplifications inappropriate. This is even more of a concern if a model is used\noutside the environment for which it was designed. Banks may do this\nintentionally as they apply existing models to new products or markets, or\ninadvertently as market conditions or customer behavior changes. Decision\nmakers need to understand the limitations of a model to avoid using it in ways\nthat are not consistent with the original intent. Limitations come in part from\nweaknesses in the model due to its various shortcomings, approximations, and\nuncertainties. Limitations are also a consequence of assumptions underlying a\nmodel that may restrict the scope to a limited set of specific circumstances and\nsituations.\nModel risk should be managed like other types of risk. Banks should identify the sources\nof risk and assess the magnitude. Model risk increases with greater model complexity,\nhigher uncertainty about inputs and assumptions, broader use, and larger potential impact.\nBanks should consider risk from individual models and in the aggregate. Aggregate\nmodel risk is affected by interaction and dependencies among models; reliance on\ncommon assumptions, data, or methodologies; and any other factors that could adversely\naffect several models and their outputs at the same time. With an understanding of the\nsource and magnitude of model risk in place, the next step is to manage it properly.\nA guiding principle for managing model risk is \"effective challenge\" of models, that is,\ncritical analysis by objective, informed parties who can identify model limitations and\nassumptions and produce appropriate changes. Effective challenge depends on a\ncombination of incentives, competence, and influence. Incentives to provide effective\nchallenge to models are stronger when there is greater separation of that challenge from\nthe model development process and when challenge is supported by well-designed\ncompensation practices and corporate culture. Competence is a key to effectiveness since\ntechnical knowledge and modeling skills are necessary to conduct appropriate analysis\nand critique. Finally, challenge may fail to be effective without the influence to ensure\nthat actions are taken to address model issues. Such influence comes from a combination\nof explicit authority, stature within the organization, and commitment and support from\nhigher levels of management.\nEven with skilled modeling and robust validation, model risk cannot be eliminated, so\nother tools should be used to manage model risk effectively. Among these are\nestablishing limits on model use, monitoring model performance, adjusting or revising\nmodels over time, and supplementing model results with other analysis and information.\nInformed conservatism, in either the inputs or the design of a model or through explicit [Page Break]\nadjustments to outputs, can be an effective tool, though not an excuse to avoid improving\nmodels.\nAs is generally the case with other risks, materiality is an important consideration in\nmodel risk management. Another essential element is a sound model validation process. A third element is\ngovernance, which sets an effective framework with defined roles and responsibilities for\nclear communication of model limitations and assumptions, as well as the authority to\nrestrict model usage.   "text": "The third core element of the validation process is outcomes analysis, a comparison of\nmodel outputs to corresponding actual outcomes. The precise nature of the comparison\ndepends on the objectives of a model, and might include an assessment of the accuracy of\nestimates or forecasts, an evaluation of rank-ordering ability, or other appropriate tests. In\nall cases, such comparisons help to evaluate model performance, by establishing expected\nranges for those actual outcomes in relation to the intended objectives and assessing the\nreasons for observed variation between the two. If outcomes analysis produces evidence\nof poor performance, the bank should take action to address those issues. Outcomes\nanalysis typically relies on statistical tests or other quantitative measures. It can also [Page Break]\ninclude expert judgment to check the intuition behind the outcomes and confirm that the\nresults make sense. When a model itself relies on expert judgment, quantitative outcomes\nanalysis helps to evaluate the quality of that judgment. Outcomes analysis should be\nconducted on an ongoing basis to test whether the model continues to perform in line\nwith design objectives and business uses.\nA variety of quantitative and qualitative testing and analytical techniques can be used in\noutcomes analysis. The choice of technique should be based on the model's\nmethodology, its complexity, data availability, and the magnitude of potential model risk\nto the bank. The comparison is generally done using expected\nranges or statistical confidence intervals around the model forecasts. When outcomes fall\noutside those intervals, the bank should analyze the discrepancies and investigate the\ncauses that are significant in terms of magnitude or frequency. The objective of the\nanalysis is to determine whether differences stem from the omission of material factors\nfrom the model, whether they arise from errors with regard to other aspects of model\nspecification such as interaction terms or assumptions of linearity, or whether they are\npurely random and thus consistent with acceptable model performance. Significant\ndeviation in expected versus actual performance and unexplained volatility in the profits\nand losses of trading activities may indicate that hedging and pricing relationships are not\nadequately measured by a given approach. {"markdown":"Sound development practice includes a critical assessment of data quality, relevance, and inputs, and this section records that assessment for the splits underlying the credit_default package at version 1.0. [[reg:SR26-2:IV.1]]

### 3.1 Split sizes and missingness

The training split holds 3500 [[art:2510d49d:profile.train.n]] rows and the test split holds 1500 [[art:2193cf5f:profile.test.n]] rows.
The largest missing fraction of any column in the training split is 0 [[art:050a3099:profile.train.missing.max]].
The largest missing fraction of any column in the test split is likewise 0 [[art:f813848d:profile.test.missing.max]].
Because both splits are fully populated, the difference in missingness between them is nil and leaves the tolerated between-split gap of 0.1 [[art:9cce25ea:threshold.D1.missing_gap]] unapproached.
No imputation behaviour therefore differs between the split the model learned on and the split it was scored on, which removes one common route by which a holdout can flatter a model.

### 3.2 Population and characteristic stability

The largest population stability index measured from the training split against the test split, with the score included among the measured quantities, is 0.01095 [[art:381b2570:psi.max]], against a bound of 0.25 [[art:278b9016:threshold.S1.psi]].
The package declares the same stability ceiling of 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]], so the declared and applied bounds agree and no reconciliation between them is needed.

  "heading": "Overview of Model Risk Management",
  "text": "For the purposes of this document, the term model refers to a quantitative method,\nsystem, or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories,\ntechniques, and assumptions to process input data into quantitative estimates. A model\nconsists of three components: an information input component, which delivers\nassumptions and data to the model; a processing component, which transforms inputs into\nestimates; and a reporting component, which translates the estimates into useful business\ninformation. Models meeting this definition might be used for analyzing business\nstrategies, informing business decisions, identifying and measuring risks, valuing\nexposures, instruments or positions, conducting stress testing, assessing adequacy of\ncapital, managing client assets, measuring compliance with internal limits, maintaining\nthe formal control apparatus of the bank, or meeting financial or regulatory reporting\nrequirements and issuing public disclosures. The definition of model also covers\nquantitative approaches whose inputs are partially or wholly qualitative or based on\nexpert judgment, provided that the output is quantitative in nature. Model quality can\nbe measured in many ways: precision, accuracy, discriminatory power, robustness,\nstability, and reliability, to name a few. Models are never perfect, and the appropriate\nmetrics of quality, and the effort that should be put into improving quality, depend on the\nsituation. For example, precision and accuracy are relevant for models that forecast future\nvalues, while discriminatory power applies to models that rank order risks. In all\nsituations, it is important to understand a model's capabilities and limitations given its\nsimplifications and assumptions.\nThe use of models invariably presents model risk, which is the potential for adverse\nconsequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports.\nModel risk can lead to financial loss, poor business and strategic decision making, or\ndamage to a bank's reputation. Model risk occurs primarily for two reasons:\n\u2022 The model may have fundamental errors and may produce inaccurate outputs\nwhen viewed against the design objective and intended business uses. The\nmathematical calculation and quantification exercise underlying any model\ngenerally involves application of theory, choice of sample design and numerical\nroutines, selection of inputs and estimation, and implementation in information\nsystems. Errors can occur at any point from design through implementation. In\naddition, shortcuts, simplifications, or approximations used to manage\ncomplicated problems could compromise the integrity and reliability of outputs [Page Break]\nfrom those calculations. Finally, the quality of model outputs depends on the\nquality of input data and assumptions, and errors in inputs or incorrect\nassumptions will lead to inaccurate outputs.\n\u2022 The model may be used incorrectly or inappropriately. Even a fundamentally\nsound model producing accurate outputs consistent with the design objective of\nthe model may exhibit high model risk if it is misapplied or misused. Models by\ntheir nature are simplifications of reality, and real-world events may prove those\nsimplifications inappropriate. This is even more of a concern if a model is used\noutside the environment for which it was designed. Banks may do this\nintentionally as they apply existing models to new products or markets, or\ninadvertently as market conditions or customer behavior changes. Decision\nmakers need to understand the limitations of a model to avoid using it in ways\nthat are not consistent with the original intent. Limitations come in part from\nweaknesses in the model due to its various shortcomings, approximations, and\nuncertainties. Limitations are also a consequence of assumptions underlying a\nmodel that may restrict the scope to a limited set of specific circumstances and\nsituations.\nModel risk should be managed like other types of risk. Banks should identify the sources\nof risk and assess the magnitude. Model risk increases with greater model complexity,\nhigher uncertainty about inputs and assumptions, broader use, and larger potential impact.\nBanks should consider risk from individual models and in the aggregate. Aggregate\nmodel risk is affected by interaction and dependencies among models; reliance on\ncommon assumptions, data, or methodologies; and any other factors that could adversely\naffect several models and their outputs at the same time. With an understanding of the\nsource and magnitude of model risk in place, the next step is to manage it properly.\nA guiding principle for managing model risk is \"effective challenge\" of models, that is,\ncritical analysis by objective, informed parties who can identify model limitations and\nassumptions and produce appropriate changes. Effective challenge depends on a\ncombination of incentives, competence, and influence. Incentives to provide effective\nchallenge to models are stronger when there is greater separation of that challenge from\nthe model development process and when challenge is supported by well-designed\ncompensation practices and corporate culture. Competence is a key to effectiveness since\ntechnical knowledge and modeling skills are necessary to conduct appropriate analysis\nand critique. Finally, challenge may fail to be effective without the influence to ensure\nthat actions are taken to address model issues. Such influence comes from a combination\nof explicit authority, stature within the organization, and commitment and support from\nhigher levels of management.\nEven with skilled modeling and robust validation, model risk cannot be eliminated, so\nother tools should be used to manage model risk effectively. Among these are\nestablishing limits on model use, monitoring model performance, adjusting or revising\nmodels over time, and supplementing model results with other analysis and information.\nInformed conservatism, in either the inputs or the design of a model or through explicit [Page Break]\nadjustments to outputs, can be an effective tool, though not an excuse to avoid improving\nmodels.\nAs is generally the case with other risks, materiality is an important consideration in\nmodel risk management. However,\nwhere models and model output have a material impact on business decisions, including\ndecisions related to risk management and capital and liquidity planning, and where model\nfailure would have a particularly harmful impact on a bank's financial condition, a bank's\nmodel risk management framework should be more extensive and rigorous.\nModel risk management begins with robust model development, implementation, and\nuse. Another essential element is a sound model validation process. A third element is\ngovernance, which sets an effective framework with defined roles and responsibilities for\nclear communication of model limitations and assumptions, as well as the authority to\nrestrict model usage.   "heading": "Outcomes Analysis",
  "text": "The third core element of the validation process is outcomes analysis, a comparison of\nmodel outputs to corresponding actual outcomes. The precise nature of the comparison\ndepends on the objectives of a model, and might include an assessment of the accuracy of\nestimates or forecasts, an evaluation of rank-ordering ability, or other appropriate tests. In\nall cases, such comparisons help to evaluate model performance, by establishing expected\nranges for those actual outcomes in relation to the intended objectives and assessing the\nreasons for observed variation between the two. If outcomes analysis produces evidence\nof poor performance, the bank should take action to address those issues. Outcomes\nanalysis typically relies on statistical tests or other quantitative measures. It can also [Page Break]\ninclude expert judgment to check the intuition behind the outcomes and confirm that the\nresults make sense. When a model itself relies on expert judgment, quantitative outcomes\nanalysis helps to evaluate the quality of that judgment. Outcomes analysis should be\nconducted on an ongoing basis to test whether the model continues to perform in line\nwith design objectives and business uses.\nA variety of quantitative and qualitative testing and analytical techniques can be used in\noutcomes analysis. The choice of technique should be based on the model's\nmethodology, its complexity, data availability, and the magnitude of potential model risk\nto the bank. Outcomes analysis should involve a range of tests because any individual test\nwill have weaknesses. For example, some tests are better at checking a model's ability to\nrank-order or segment observations on a relative basis, whereas others are better at\nchecking absolute forecast accuracy. Tests should be designed for each situation, as not\nall will be effective or feasible in every circumstance, and attention should be paid to\nchoosing the appropriate type of outcomes analysis for a particular model.\nModels are regularly adjusted to take into account new data or techniques, or because of\ndeterioration in performance. Parallel outcomes analysis, under which both the original\nand adjusted models' forecasts are tested against realized outcomes, provides an\nimportant test of such model adjustments. If the adjusted model does not outperform the\noriginal model, developers, users, and reviewers should realize that additional changes\u2014\nor even a wholesale redesign\u2014are likely necessary before the adjusted model replaces\nthe original one.\nBack-testing is one form of outcomes analysis; specifically, it involves the comparison of\nactual outcomes with model forecasts during a sample time period not used in model\ndevelopment and at an observation frequency that matches the forecast horizon or\nperformance window of the model. The comparison is generally done using expected\nranges or statistical confidence intervals around the model forecasts. When outcomes fall\noutside those intervals, the bank should analyze the discrepancies and investigate the\ncauses that are significant in terms of magnitude or frequency. The objective of the\nanalysis is to determine whether differences stem from the omission of material factors\nfrom the model, whether they arise from errors with regard to other aspects of model\nspecification such as interaction terms or assumptions of linearity, or whether they are\npurely random and thus consistent with acceptable model performance. Analysis of in-\nsample fit and of model performance in holdout samples (data set aside and not used to\nestimate the original model) are important parts of model development but are not\nsubstitutes for back-testing.\nA well-known example of back-testing is the evaluation of value-at-risk (VaR), in which\nactual profit and loss is compared with a model forecast loss distribution. Significant\ndeviation in expected versus actual performance and unexplained volatility in the profits\nand losses of trading activities may indicate that hedging and pricing relationships are not\nadequately measured by a given approach. Along with measuring the frequency of losses\nin excess of a single VaR percentile estimator, banks should use other tests, such as [Page Break]\nassessing any clustering of exceptions and checking the distribution of losses against\nother estimated percentiles.\nAnalysis of the results of even high-quality and well-designed back-testing can pose\nchallenges, since it is not a straightforward, mechanical process that always produces\nunambiguous results. The purpose is to test the model, not individual forecast values.\nBack-testing may entail analysis of a large number of forecasts over different conditions\nat a point in time or over multiple time periods. Statistical testing is essential in such\ncases, yet such testing can pose challenges in both the choice of appropriate tests and the\ninterpretation of results; banks should support and document both the choice of tests and\nthe interpretation of results.\nModels with long forecast horizons should be back-tested, but given the amount of time it\nwould take to accumulate the necessary data, that testing should be supplemented by\nevaluation over shorter periods. Banks should employ outcomes analysis consisting of\n\"early warning\" metrics designed to measure performance beginning very shortly after\nmodel introduction and trend analysis of performance over time. These outcomes analysis\ntools are not substitutes for back-testing, which should still be performed over the longer\ntime period, but rather very important complements.\nOutcomes analysis and the other elements of the validation process may reveal significant\nerrors or inaccuracies in model development or outcomes that consistently fall outside the\nbank's predetermined thresholds of acceptability. In such cases, model adjustment,\nrecalibration, or redevelopment is warranted. Adjustments and recalibration should be\ngoverned by the principle of conservatism and should undergo independent review.\nMaterial changes in model structure or technique, and all model redevelopment, should\nbe subject to validation activities of appropriate range and rigor before implementation.\nAt times banks may have a limited ability to use key model validation tools like back-\ntesting or sensitivity analysis for various reasons, such as lack of data or of price\nobservability. In those cases, even more attention should be paid to the model's\nlimitations when considering the appropriateness of model usage, and senior management\nshould be fully informed of those limitations when using the models for decision making.\nSuch scrutiny should be applied to individual models and models in the aggregate."

  "heading": "Conceptual Soundness",
  "text": "Validating  conceptual  soundness  involves  assessing  and  documenting  model  design\n(including  key  modeling  choices,  assumptions,  qualitative  judgments,  and  data  selection),\nconstruction,  and  developmental  testing. Sound  practice  subjects\nmodeling  aspects  to  critical  analysis  by  evaluating  both  the  quality  and  extent  of  developmental\nevidence."
 },
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR26-2:IV.1]]",
  "heading": "Model Development",
  "text": "Sound  model  development  activities  are  aligned  with  model  purpose,  business  use,  and\nbanking  organization  policy.  Model  development  is  not  purely  a  technical  exercise.  The\ndeveloper\u2019s  judgment  influences  the  model\u2019s  conceptual  design  and  soundness,  inputs,\nassumptions,  and  methodology,  all  of  which  affect  a  model\u2019s  inherent  risk.  Because  model\ndevelopment  is  often  multidisciplinary,  tailored  to  actual  use,  and  involves  significant\nsubjectivity  throughout  its  lifecycle,  sound  development  practices  are  important  for  effective\nmodel  risk  management.\nAn  effective  development  process  generally  begins  with  a  clear  statement  of  purpose  to\nmaximize  the  likelihood  that  model  development  is  aligned  with  the  intended  use.  This\nfundamental  step  supports  decision-making  throughout  the  development  lifecycle,  including  the\nselection  of  data,  methodologies,  and  testing  approaches.\nInput  from  model  users  can  enhance  model  development  by  providing  business  context\nand  practical  insights.  Business  managers  affected  by  model  outcomes  may  raise  questions  about\nthe  methods  or  assumptions,  particularly  when  the  outcomes  are  unexpected.  Constructive\nengagement  around  model  design  and  assumptions  strengthens  both  model  understanding  and\nmodel  quality.\nModel  testing  is  a  core  component  of  model  development  that  evaluates  whether  a  model\nperforms  as  intended.  Testing  may  include  a  range  of  activities,  from  out-of-sample  and  out-of-\ntime  testing,  to  a  comparison  of  alternative  assumptions  and  methodologies,  to  a  critical\nassessment  of  data  quality,  relevance,  and  inputs.  Testing  may  be  performed  by  model\ndevelopers  in  collaboration  with  model  users.  The  specific  approach  depends  on  the  model\u2019s\ncharacteristics.  The  rigor  of  effective  testing  is  commensurate  with  model  complexity  and\nmateriality.  For  models  that  have  relatively  less  material  impact  or  for  banking  organizations\nwith  relatively  less  complex  operations,  model  testing  may  be  more  limited  in  scope."

 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR26-2:V.1.b]]",
  "heading": "Outcomes Analysis",
  "text": "Outcomes  analysis  compares  model  outputs  to  corresponding  real-world  outcomes  to\nassess  model  performance  relative  to  model  objectives  and  business  use. In  such  cases,  model\nadjustment,  recalibration,  or  redevelopment  may  be  warranted.\nOutcomes  analysis  can  take  many  forms,  including  testing  conducted  during  model\ndevelopment,  reports  or  analysis  performed  as  part  of  ongoing  monitoring,  or  standalone\nactivities  such  as  back-testing  or  outlier  analysis.  A  banking  organization\u2019s  approach  depends  on\nthe  model\u2019s  objectives,  methodology,  and  data  availability.   "heading": "Internal Audit",
  "text": "A  bank's  internal  audit  function  should  assess  the  overall  effectiveness  of  the  model  risk\nmanagement  framework,  including  the  framework's  ability  to  address  both  types  of\nmodel  risk  described  in  Section  III,  for  individual  models  and  in  the  aggregate.
